title: Masei: cities of refuge (Numbers 35:9–15)
hookLine: six cities where one who killed by accident could flee

lines: AN ACCIDENT, AND NOBODY MEANT IT.
cards: A second of distraction on a wet road. A ladder that wasn't tied down. An accident that ends a life, and nobody meant it.
In the ancient world, that wasn't the end of the story. A relative of the person who died might come looking for blood. The Torah even has a name for him: the avenger of blood.
It doesn't pretend that anger away. But as the people stand at the edge of the land, it sets aside six cities, built for the person who did the worst thing they never meant to do.

teach.h: IR MIKLAT: A CITY OF REFUGE.
teach.b: In paraphrase: when you cross the Jordan, choose cities to be cities of refuge, so that someone who kills a person by accident can flee there. Six in all: three east of the Jordan, three in the land of Canaan.

teach.h: SIX CITIES, OPEN TO THE STRANGER.
teach.b: They're open to everyone: to Israelites, and to the stranger and the settler living among them. The Hebrew is ir miklat, a city of refuge, of shelter.

There the person was safe from the avenger, and would have a proper trial. If the death was found to be an accident, they lived in the city of refuge until the death of the high priest, then could go home.
The rabbis made this law humane in surprising detail.
The Talmud says the roads to the cities had to be kept in good repair, and at every crossroads a sign read refuge, refuge, so a frightened person running for their life would never take a wrong turn.
The cities needed water and markets, and had to be neither too small nor too crowded.

teach.h: A TEACHER GOES WITH HIS STUDENT.
teach.b: If a student had to flee there, the Talmud says, his teacher went with him, so he wouldn't be cut off from learning.
And the mothers of the high priests, it says, brought food and clothing to the people in the cities, so they wouldn't pray for the high priest to die. None of this pretends the death didn't happen.
The person still lived away from home for as long as that high priest lived. But a mistake didn't have to end in another death. There was a road, signposted, to somewhere safe.

how: The cities of refuge are read in the portion of Masei in midsummer, and their laws are studied in the Talmud tractate Makkot, which describes the roads, signs and care for those who fled there.

games.q: your student killed someone by accident and has fled to a city of refuge. he'll be there for years. what do you do?
o: go and live there with him.
wait for him to come home.
games.why: the Talmud says the teacher goes with the student into exile, so he isn't cut off from learning.

practice: Think of someone who hurt you, or others, without meaning to: a careless word, an honest mistake with real consequences.
Let the part of you that wants them to pay be there, then ask whether you could leave a road to refuge open for them, not pretending it didn't happen, but not chasing them either.
